title: SKP Business / Pipeline
description: Business / pipeline counters across the three services that emit domain meters (orchestrator / keeper / processor), plus the WebApi represented by ASP.NET Core request metrics only (it registers no domain meter - BPD-03). The two template variables are populated from the process_runtime_dotnet_* family emitted by OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.Runtime 1.15.0 on net8.0 (research F-1) - the one instrumentation every service class shares. A future net9.0 upgrade would rename that family to dotnet_* and blank both dropdowns; scripts/phase-87-dashboard-lint.ps1 rule S8 hard-fails on any dotnet_* reference so that regression surfaces hermetically in ~5s instead of as a silently empty dashboard.

panels.title: Orchestrator consumed vs sent (conservation)
panels.description: Messages the orchestrator took in versus messages it sent out. The two lines should move together - that is the conservation relationship, and it is the quickest way to see whether the orchestrator is keeping up. Note that sent counts every destination, not just processors, so it normally runs above consumed. Investigate when the lines diverge and stay diverged, or when consumed keeps rising while sent flattens: the orchestrator is taking in work it is not passing on. Both lines at zero simply means the pipeline is idle.

panels.title: Keeper consumed vs sent (conservation)
panels.description: Recovery messages the keeper took in versus sent back out. Expected: flat zero on a healthy stack, because these counters only move during an actual recovery event - an empty-looking panel here is good news, not a broken panel. Investigate when the two diverge during a recovery: messages entered the recovery path and did not come out. Both lines are deliberately guarded so this reads 0 rather than No data.

panels.title: Processor consumed vs sent by image (conservation)
panels.description: Work each processor image took in versus results it sent back, split by image identity. The lines should track closely. Investigate a sustained gap, meaning work is being consumed without producing results, or one image flatlining while others continue, which isolates the fault to that image. Split by image identity rather than service name because every processor pod reports the same placeholder service name and cannot be distinguished that way.

panels.title: Orchestrator sends minus processor pickups (structural - read the trend)
panels.description: Every message the orchestrator sent, minus every message processors picked up. These are deliberately NOT equal and this number is NOT a loss count. The orchestrator sends to processors, to its own result-post queue, and to the keeper, so only about half its sends are bound for a processor - measured at a ratio of 1.8 to 1 on this stack. The difference therefore normally sits close to the processor pickup count itself and grows with traffic. Read the trend, not the value: investigate when it departs sharply from its recent level, which means the two tiers have stopped moving together. It cannot be made to read zero without a code change to label send destinations, so it is shown in a neutral colour rather than as a red alarm.

panels.title: Per-processor dispatch gap
panels.description: Per processor identity, the rate the orchestrator sent work minus the rate that processor picked it up. Like the panel above it, this does not settle at zero - the orchestrator sends to destinations other than processors, so a positive offset is structural. What matters is that each identity holds a steady offset. Investigate one identity drifting away from the others, or a line that climbs and keeps climbing: that processor is falling behind the rate work is being dispatched to it.

panels.title: Orchestrator unresolved steps in range
panels.description: Workflow steps the orchestrator could not match to a destination and gave up on. Expected: 0, shown in green - which is deliberately different from No data. Investigate at 1 or more: each count is a step that entered the pipeline and never reached a processor, so work has been lost silently. Cross-check the orchestrator logs in the same window for a Dangling next-step id entry to identify which step.

panels.title: Processor dropped spawns in range
panels.description: Follow-on work a processor tried to create and failed to hand off after exhausting its retries. Expected: 0, in green. Investigate at 1 or more: the parent step succeeded but its child work never entered the pipeline, so the workflow is quietly incomplete and nothing downstream will report it. Check the processor logs in the same window and the broker health, since exhausted retries usually mean the broker was unreachable.

panels.title: Keeper consumed - sent gap in range
panels.description: Recovery messages that entered the keeper and did not come back out during the selected window. Expected: 0, in green. Investigate at 1 or more: something entered the recovery path and was neither reinjected nor cleanly discarded, which is the one failure mode that can lose a message the pipeline had already accepted. On a healthy stack both underlying counters stay at zero, so this reads 0 for the ordinary reason that no recovery was needed.

panels.title: Keeper L2 probe heartbeat
panels.description: The keeper liveness probe against its Redis projection - a genuine heartbeat, unlike the other keeper panels on this dashboard. Typical: a flat 0.4 probes/sec, and remarkably steady, measured between 0.4001 and 0.4005. Investigate any dip toward zero or a gap in the line: the keeper has stopped probing, meaning it is wedged or has lost Redis, and it will not be able to recover messages if asked to. This is the first panel to check when asking whether the keeper is alive.

panels.title: WebApi request rate by route
panels.description: Incoming HTTP requests per second, split by route. Near zero is expected on this stack when nothing is driving traffic, because the pipeline runs on its own schedule rather than on HTTP. Investigate an unfamiliar route appearing, or a route rate jumping with no matching change on the pipeline panels. Health-check requests are dropped by the metrics collector and never appear here, so their absence is not a fault.

panels.title: WebApi p95 request duration by route
panels.description: The slowest 5 percent of requests per route: 95 of every 100 requests finished faster than this. Read it per route - one slow route is usually a code problem, whereas every route slowing together points at resource pressure, so check the runtime dashboard GC and thread-pool panels next. Empty when no traffic is flowing. This stack has no established latency baseline yet, so compare against what this panel showed yesterday rather than against an absolute target.

panels.title: WebApi status-code mix
panels.description: HTTP responses per second grouped by status code. Healthy: 2xx only. Investigate any sustained 5xx, which is a server-side fault, and a rise in 4xx, which usually means a caller is sending something malformed rather than the server being broken. The 5xx ratio panel beside this one is the quicker read for severity.

panels.title: WebApi 5xx ratio
panels.description: The share of requests failing with a server error, as a percentage. Expected: 0 percent. Investigate anything above 0 - on a stack carrying this little HTTP traffic, even a single failure is worth opening the logs for. Deliberately guarded so it reads 0 percent rather than No data when there are no errors at all, which is the normal case here.

panels.title: WebApi in-flight requests and Kestrel connections
panels.description: Requests currently being processed, and TCP connections currently open. Typical: 0 for both, since this WebApi is idle unless something is driving it. Investigate in-flight requests staying above zero while the request rate is flat - requests are arriving and not completing, so something is hanging. Connections outnumbering in-flight requests is normal, because clients hold connections open between calls.
